recordings.text: What changed: a single piece now sits where it touches several targets at once. It follows that one reply is unlikely to cover all of them.
One detail is different after this move: an enemy piece can now reach a square from which several targets are hit together.
The stronger move would have set one piece against several targets. After this move, that arrangement never appears.
A piece now stands on the line between its king and an attacker. Stepping off that line is no longer a legal option for it.
The piece in front of the king has become pinnable. Once the pin arrives, leaving that line stops being legal.
With the stronger move, an enemy piece would have been fixed in front of its king. As it is, that piece keeps every option.
The front piece on the line is under attack now. When it steps away, what was standing behind it becomes the target.
After this move, two pieces are lined up so the other side can skewer them. The front one would have to step away, leaving the rear one exposed.
A skewer sat inside the stronger move: pressure on the front piece, the real target behind it. After this move the line remains untouched.
The piece doing the defending has been captured. Whatever depended on it has lost that cover.
A defender has become capturable. If it is taken, the piece it was covering no longer has that support.
The stronger move would have captured a defender and stripped cover from what it guarded. That defender is still standing.
The king's exits are occupied by its own pieces, and its last rank has become the point of attack.
After this move the king has no square off its back rank, and a mate along that rank is available to the other side.
The enemy king had no way off its back rank; its own pieces were in the way. The mate that this allowed was not played.
The pawn has moved a step nearer promotion. It follows that the defense has fewer moves in hand.
A route toward promotion has opened for an enemy pawn. Each further step it takes will require an answer.
The stronger move would have carried a pawn closer to its promotion square. In this position that pawn is where it was.
The front piece has stepped off the line, and the piece that was behind it now attacks along it.
One enemy piece now screens another. Once the screening piece moves, the one behind it attacks down the opened line.
The stronger move would have uncovered an attack by moving a front piece off its line. That line has stayed shut.
One move, and now there are threats in two places. It follows that a single reply rarely deals with both.
After this move, the other side could create two threats with a single move.
The stronger move would have produced two threats together. No such pair arises from this one.
The defender has been drawn away from its job, and what it was covering is uncovered now.
One defender can now be lured away from what it was covering.
Under the stronger move, a defender would have been pulled away from what it guards. Here that defender is undisturbed.
The piece that was captured had no defender, so there is no recapture available.
With the stronger move, an enemy piece without protection could have been taken. It is still standing.
After this move one piece stands without protection, and the other side can take it with nothing coming back.
This piece was the only real defender of another. It has gone elsewhere, so the piece it guarded is now open to capture.
A threat appeared with the opponent's last move. This reply leaves the threat as it was, so a piece is still capturable.
The exchange has a second half. The recapture removes a more valuable piece, so the material count falls overall.
One minor piece is no longer at home; it has been brought into play.
With the alternative, a minor piece would have been developed. Here that piece is still at home.
The rook now stands on a file that holds no pawn of either color.
The alternative would have put a rook on a file free of pawns of both colors.
The rook's file now has no pawn of its own color and at least one enemy pawn. That makes it semi-open.
The alternative would have placed a rook where none of its own pawns block the file and enemy pawns still stand.
A pawn has become passed. Neither on its file nor on the two beside it is there an enemy pawn ahead.
The alternative would have given a pawn a clear path, with no enemy pawn ahead on its own file or on either side.
The passed pawn stands a square further on than before.
The alternative pushed the passed pawn on. Here it keeps its square.
A pawn has become isolated: neither neighboring file holds a pawn of its color any longer.
The alternative would have isolated a pawn, leaving both neighboring files without a pawn of its color.
Before this move, a piece had no defender. Now it has one.
The alternative would have supplied a defender to a piece that has none at the moment.
A piece has lost its last defender. The weakness is real; it does not on its own show the piece can be won.
The alternative would have taken away a piece's last defender. By itself, that would not have shown it could be won.
The king has one more legal square than before. Something on the board changed to make that room.
The alternative would have given the king one additional legal square.
The king has castled. It moved two squares, and the rook has crossed to its other side.
Castling was available, moving king and rook together in a single turn.
Before this capture there was a bishop pair; now there is not. That side's remaining bishop covers only one square color.
With the alternative, a bishop would have been captured and the opposing pair would have ended.
Before this move the pawns stood on different files; now two of the same color share one. They are doubled.
The alternative would have left two pawns doubled up on a single file.
Something decisive has shifted. From here a forced checkmate is in the other side's hands, and the reason lies in the moves before this one.
The mating line that existed before this move no longer exists after it. A forced checkmate went unplayed.
Material has been offered. The checked line shows the idea survives even if the offer is accepted.
Among the examined moves, only this one keeps the position playable. Every other one loses.
Among the examined moves, this is the one that keeps the advantage. All the others lose.
The first change to note: on its next move, the other side has a capture available.
The strongest reply arrives as a check. The king's safety now comes before anything else.
What the engine would play here is something different. After the strongest reply, the two lines go different ways.
Compared with the engine's top move, part of the value is gone. Follow the reply to see where the gap opens.
Strong. Compared with the engine's choices, very little value has changed hands.
Sound. The engine leans toward another move, yet most of the position's value is still in place.
This move is one a recognized opening contains.
The game moves outside the known opening at this point. From here, the position is unfamiliar.
After the earlier error, the position has become playable again. That is the change worth recording.
The earlier error has stopped being decisive, and the game is playable once more. The other side's mistakes played a part in that.
The opponent's last move left something available. This move collects it.
The opponent's last move left something available. This reply does not take it, and a stronger answer existed.
This issue is not new in this game; it came up once already. Placed side by side, the two moments share a pattern.
A piece lost its protection earlier on. That protection has returned.
Small concessions keep accumulating, and this move is another of them. One by one they are minor; together they have shifted the position.
From that point until the recorded win, the advantage stayed in place and was never handed back.
This issue is not limited to this game; other saved games contain it as well. The positions share a common thread.
Checkmate. No legal move remains for the king, and the game has ended.
Checkmate. Every legal move is gone for the defending king. The decisions leading here are where things changed.
A draw. The result is fixed, though the decisions along the way remain worth examining.
Look at the position as it stands, then choose a move.
Not the answer. Look again at what the last move changed.
The attempt went through without a result. Enter the move once again.
According to the saved engine analysis, a forced checkmate is now in the hands of the side that played this move.
The saved engine analysis records that this move leaves its own side facing a forced checkmate.
Set the material at the end of the saved line beside the material at its start: the side that played this move has gained.
Set the material at the end of the saved line beside the material at its start: the side that played this move has lost some.
This move is accepted. Nothing in the moves shown gives a clear tactical reason, and none is supposed.
The exercise does not take this move, and nothing in the moves shown points to a clear tactical reason. Look over what changed once more.
It appears among the saved answers, which are the standard in this exercise.
None of the saved answers is this move. That does not rule it out as sound chess.
Take note of the move and its reason, and continue with the next position.
Correct. What transfers to other positions is the reason, more than the move itself.
The practice has been recorded, and the review schedule is the same as before.
Solved. For now, this recall stays marked as relearning.
This is how the position looked before any of these moves.
One move is played. Note what is different afterward.
Check. Until it is answered, nothing else matters.
The check has been answered; the king is clear.
The pawn has reached the last rank and been replaced by a new piece.
After the promotion, the new piece is giving check.
After the promotion, the position is checkmate.
After the promotion, its own king is out of check as well.
A capture. There is one piece fewer on the board.
After the capture, the king is in check.
After the capture, the position is checkmate.
After the capture, the king is out of check.
With a capture, the pawn arrives on the last rank and is replaced by a new piece.
After capturing and promoting, the new piece is giving check.
After capturing and promoting, the position is checkmate.
After capturing and promoting, its own king is out of check.
After castling, the opposing king is in check.
After castling, the position is checkmate.
A fork in operation: one piece threatens several targets and, a little later, captures one. By the end of this example there is a net material gain.
The marked capture is not legal here. This piece is pinned, and moving it would expose its king.
Pinned to its king, the attacked piece only has moves that keep that king shielded.
No recapture comes, because each defender is pinned to its king. That is why the capture is possible, and the line shown ends with more material.
The pinned piece cannot leave its line while its king stands behind. Before the sequence ends, it is captured.
Once the front piece steps off the line, the one that stood behind it is captured.
A check sends the king off the line, and the same attacker then captures what was behind it.
The lone defender is captured, and after it, the piece it was protecting.
The defender is drawn away from where it stood, and what it was covering is captured next.
The blocking piece steps off the line; the piece behind it then captures along the opening it left.
One piece leaves the line, and check comes through the gap it left.
Double check. With two pieces giving check, only a king move is possible.
Two targets, two attackers: the moving piece threatens one, and the line it opened threatens the other. The piece behind collects.
Promotion. When this example finishes, that side is also ahead on material.
A piece without protection is taken, and the capturing side finishes this example with more material.
A relative pin had been holding the attacking piece. The opponent's previous move lifted it, and the piece captures a target that never moved, in the line shown.
The other side is permitted the marked reply. Play it on the board and note what changes.
Before moving, check that no piece is left to be taken without a recapture.
Before a quiet move, check whether any enemy piece has lost its protection.
Among the forcing moves, notice whether one piece could land on two valuable targets.
Before a pinned piece moves, consider what it shields, whether that is the king or a piece of greater value.
Note what stands behind the first target. A more valuable piece may be on the same line.
Before a defender is traded, note what it is protecting.
When a piece moves off a line, note what that line now reaches.
Note any single move that creates two threats, including checks and lines it opens.
If a back-rank defender is about to move, first confirm the king will still have an escape square.
Note how many squares a pawn still needs to promote, and which of its moves demand a reply.
Before a defender moves, note which pieces rely on it.
Before capturing, weigh what is won against what the recapture would remove.
Note whether a forcing exchange could draw a defender away from a second task.
Here the saved answers are the measure. Outside them, a legal move may still be sound.
The line uses strong replies. Those are not the only ones possible.
Within the line shown, material is counted from that line's own first position. The written explanation gives the values used for each piece.
No simple tactical reason can be read from the saved line, and no positional one is supposed. Play it out and note how each reply changes things.
The answer policy stored with this exercise determines how it is explained, and its setting is written in the notes.
Here is the opening line, each move in order.
Correct. That move belongs to your study material.
Choose a move from the opening lines you are studying.
This position appears in more than one of your chosen opening lines, and each of them offers a valid move.
Recall the move that comes next in your study material.
That move does not appear in your chosen opening lines. Try again.
That is outside your chosen lines; try again. The study was edited, so review dates are unaffected by this saved attempt.
That is outside your chosen lines; try again. The position is retired, so its review dates do not change.
Any move from this line is accepted under Mixed Due. Dedicated practice wants this specific line and no other.
Due recalls will ask for the moves of your chosen side. Where several active studies share a position, there is one card for it.
Another move needs the saved session reloaded first.
The verified line is now being played out on the board.
The record lists this attempt as revealed. The solution is still below.
Solved, after an earlier miss. The record keeps that miss as well.
Solved, and no wrong move along the way.
This puzzle asks for a different move. Moves already played correctly are still saved.
Correct. The puzzle continues with the next move.
Observe the position carefully, and move once the line is clear.
There is not enough engine analysis to explain this position, so no explanation is given.
Review paused. It continues below, or a move can be tried on the board.
Pick any move to revisit, or play one of your own on the board.
With this move, the game has entered a recognized opening.
The game stays on mapped ground; a known opening already has this move on file.
There is an entry for this move in the opening book.
Still no departure from the book.
This one is in the book too.
Even the reply sticks to the book.
The book line carries on unchanged.
One more move that the book contains.
Nothing has left the book yet.
Once more, a book move.
Still the book. That places the game; it says nothing about the move's quality.
The game begins here. Move ahead when ready, and note what each move changes.
I'm Marisol. I keep what is on the board apart from what the analysis infers, and I tell you which is which.
The position is untouched. Material is level, and no piece is under attack. That is the starting record.
A piece has been left open to capture, at an immediate cost. The position can afford it.
On the board, a piece is offered. The analysis finds the offer sound.
What changed is the material on offer. What did not change is that the position holds.
Brilliant. The sacrifice is real, and so is its soundness.
This turn carried real weight. The move's quality matched it: strong.
Great. A strong move. It arrives at a turning point, which is what lifts the grade.
Two facts to record: the timing was critical, and the move is strong.
A strong move, made where the stakes stood above the ordinary.
The move played is the engine's top choice. Observation and analysis agree here.
Best. The position after it is as good as the position allowed.
The balance is the same after this move as before it. That is what the top choice does.
The best move. Every alternative falls short of it or only equals it.
Good. Against the top choice, it comes up slightly short. The move itself is sound.
A slightly stronger move existed. That is the only thing to note here.
Good. No flaw of consequence appears in this move.
This one holds the position together, if not perfectly.
Little has changed, but something has: a slight loss of value.
Inaccuracy. Observed: a minor drop in value. Nothing more is inferred.
An inaccuracy. After this move, the position is worth a little less.
The record shows a small imprecision here, and no larger change.
A mistake. The position now stands well below where it could have been.
The drop in value is larger than an inaccuracy allows. It follows that this is a mistake.
What changed here is more than a slip. The position is markedly weaker.
Mistake. The difference from the top choice is considerable.
Before this move, there was a chance. It went unused.
This move does not collect the available gain. That is what makes it a miss.
One option here secured something definite. The move played is not that option.
For the record: a concrete chance existed on this turn, and a different move was played.
A blunder. What changed here is large, and it is costly.
Serious. This move costs a large amount, and nothing in it offsets the cost.
Before this move and after it, the position is very different. A blunder.
The damage from this move is severe. It is graded a blunder.
That move differs from the one this chapter expects. Compare the position again and choose once more.
That agrees with the chapter's intended move. The next step builds on it.
The intended move is now shown on the board. Note what it changes before continuing.
Now the moves advance automatically. Track what each one alters in the position.
Recall time: reproduce the move your preparation recorded for this position.
This branch departs from the main sequence. Notice exactly where the two diverge.
Chapter complete, with your progress recorded.
The complete game is now available. Move through it freely and return to the chapter at any point.
The lesson has to be reloaded before it can resume.
